response.text:
About mid-day, swathed in a shark-skin apron, Perth stood between forge and anvil, when moody Ahab came with a rusty leathern bag. Sparks flew as the pike-head was hammered. “Are these thy Mother Carey’s chickens, Perth? they burn; but thou—thou liv’st among them without a scorch.” “Because I am scorched all over,” said Perth; “not easily can’st thou scorch a scar.” “Well, well; no more. Thy shrunk voice sounds too calmly, sanely woeful to me. In no Paradise myself, I am impatient of all misery in others that is not mad. Thou should’st go mad, blacksmith; say, why dost thou not go mad? How can’st thou endure without being mad? Do the heavens yet hate thee, that thou can’st not go mad?”

Ahab’s voice turned: “Can’st thou smoothe almost any seams and dents?” “Aye; all but one.” Ahab leaned both hands on his shoulders, sweeping one hand across his ribbed brow: “Look ye here—here—can ye smoothe out a seam like this? if thou could’st, blacksmith, glad enough would I lay my head upon thy anvil, and feel thy heaviest hammer between my eyes. Answer!” “Oh! that is the one.” “Aye, blacksmith, it is the one; aye, man, it is unsmoothable; for though thou only see’st it here in my flesh, it has worked down into the bone of my skull—that is all wrinkles! But, away with child’s play;”

“I, too, want a harpoon made; one that a thousand yoke of fiends could not part; something that will stick in a whale like his own fin-bone. There’s the stuff.” The bag spilled gathered nail-stubbs of racing horses’ steel shoes. “The best and stubbornest stuff we work,” said Perth. “I know it, old man; these stubbs will weld together like glue from the melted bones of murderers. Quick! forge me the harpoon. And forge me first, twelve rods for its shank; then wind, and twist, and hammer these twelve together like tow-line yarns.”

A flaw rejected; then Ahab himself took the welding. The forge shot up its intense straight flame; the Parsee passed silently, and bowing over his head towards the fire, seemed invoking some curse or some blessing on the toil. But, as Ahab looked up, he slid aside. “That Parsee smells fire like a fusee; and smells of it himself, like a hot musket’s powder-pan,” muttered Stubb. The tempered shank hissed in the cask; the steam scalded Ahab’s face. “Would’st thou brand me, Perth?—have I been but forging my own branding-iron, then?” “Pray God, not that; yet I fear something. Is not this harpoon for the White Whale?” “For the white fiend!”

“Now for the barbs; thou must make them thyself. Here are my razors.” For a moment Perth eyed them; “Take them, man: I now neither shave, sup, nor pray till—” To temper: “No—no water; I want it of the true death-temper. Ahoy, there! Tashtego, Queequeg, Daggoo! Will ye give me as much blood as will cover this barb?” Dark nods: three punctures. The barbs were baptized. “Ego non baptizo te in nomine patris, sed in nomine diaboli!” deliriously howled Ahab, as the malignant iron scorchingly devoured the baptismal blood.

A hickory pole was fitted; a new tow-line strained like a harp-string—“Good! and now for the seizings.” Rope unstranded, yarns woven round the socket; the pole driven home; the line traced and bound along its length—pole, iron, and rope, like the Three Fates, made one. Ahab stalked away, the ivory leg and hickory hollowly ringing along the planks—till a light, half-bantering yet piteous sound was heard: poor Pip’s restless laugh, his strange mummeries not unmeaningly mingled with the ship’s black tragedy, and mocked it.
